gendered_labor.assessment: One source (general secondary synthesis) states women maintained fields of maize, cassava, and sweet potatoes while men hunted and fished — a Guarani-specific (not merely generically-assumed-regional) statement, but not cross-checked against a peer-reviewed ethnographic source (e.g. dedicated Mbyá or Kaiowá household-economy studies) in this research pass. Treated as provisional.

sources.citation: General secondary synthesis of Guarani gendered subsistence division (Britannica/EBSCO-derived summary).

household_authority.assessment: The only relevant documented fact is structural, not directly about authority: villages were organized into large communal houses (malocas, up to ~60 families) of patrilineally related families. This establishes a patrilineal descent pattern but does not by itself establish gendered household authority, which are not mutually exclusive in comparative lowland-South-American ethnography — not to be inferred from descent pattern alone.

sources.citation: General ethnographic description of Guarani communal-house (maloca) social organization (Britannica; Wikipedia "Guaraní people," corroborated tertiary sourcing).

gendered_legal_restrictions.assessment: Guarani religious knowledge is genuinely restricted/esoteric in the documented literature: the "Ñeʼẽ Porã Tenondé" tradition recorded by León Cadogan was described as possessed only by "the initiated," gated by trust and ritual initiation — Cadogan's own informant, Mbyá religious leader Cacique Pablo Vera, revealed it to him only after a long trusted relationship, and Cadogan was subsequently himself ritually initiated. This satisfies this project's ethical constraint (existence of a documented restriction reported as a citable fact, content not reconstructed). Whether this initiated/esoteric status carries a specific gender dimension (i.e. whether karai/religious-leader status is documented as male-restricted, open to female specialists such as a possible kunhã karai role, or something more complex) was NOT verified in this research pass and should not be assumed either way without a dedicated follow-up search.

sources.citation: Cadogan, León. Ayvu Rapyta: Textos míticos de los Mbyá-Guaraní del Guairá. Serialized in Revista de Antropología beginning 1953; discussed via Portal Guaraní and Espejo Textual secondary sourcing.
